title: Simulation Sketchbook: Works in Process
summary:
An artist’s sketchbook is one of the most precious spaces for research and experimentation. In its ideal, the sketchbook is an intimate domain where artists capture ideas, test compositions, wrestle with subjects, and scribble marginalia, engaging in an ongoing inner dialogue that audiences don’t witness.

Of course, some of these sketches do eventually make their way to the public, offering new access points for understanding these artists’ practices. From Da Vinci to Rubens, Seurat to Van Gogh, O’Keeffe to Walker, sketches reveal the essence of an artist’s pursuit at a particular moment in the raw — whether or not they ever inform the creation of a publicly presented artwork. They add new textures and tones, deepening context for artists in both personal and professional dimensions.

Sketches are also regarded as a crucial proving ground, a training hall where artists grapple with craft. When a young Degas proclaimed his intentions to become a painter, Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres purportedly told him, “Draw lines. Draw a lot of lines.” Fittingly, Degas would himself later say, “Drawing is the artist’s most direct and spontaneous expression, a species of writing: it reveals, better than does painting, [their] true personality.” 

Sketches manifest a different kind of honesty; the way a diary entry is honest, the way bedhead is honest. They are intrinsically in-process, always gesturing elsewhere.

In analog forms, sketches are highly correlated with drawing on paper. Simulation Sketchbook: Works in Process poses a simple question: what does a sketch look like for an artist working in more experimental modes like digital art and time-based media? What is a sketch when it’s not a conventional drawing?
